title: The Transposed Digit

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Twentieth Saying: The error you find is a gift. The error you hide is a trap.*

The rain had stopped, but the mud in the mill-yard remained soft, and the air held the sharp, mineral scent of wet slate and woodsmoke. Isla sat at the long oak table, her field-book open to the western traverse, while Mags Okoro stood behind her, holding a slate of calculations. The iron pot tied to Mags's pack clinked softly against the wood as she shifted her weight from one foot to the other.

"Check leg fourteen again," Mags said. Her voice was flat, the kind of flat that usually preceded a storm, or a very large bill.

Isla looked up from the page. "I have checked it twice, Mags. The sightglass angles are consistent, and the baseline projection holds."

"Then why does the sum not close?" Mags tapped the slate with a knuckle, a sharp, dry sound that cut through the room. "Leg fourteen. You recorded four thousand, three hundred and twenty-one links. But the computed total, derived from the other three legs and the closing angle, demands four thousand, two hundred and thirty-one."

Isla frowned, her brow furrowing as she processed the numbers in her head. "That is a discrepancy of ninety links. That is nearly sixty feet. That is impossible. I measured that leg with the chain, then verified it with the tape. It is a straight shot across the lower meadow. It does not drift."

"Neither does math," Mags said. She slid the slate across the table, the chalk dust scattering like tiny white snowflakes. "I checked the arithmetic. Three times. My porridge is thick enough to stand a spoon upright, Isla, but my arithmetic is thinner than that. I have recalculated the sine ratios. I have checked the declination correction. The numbers are telling the truth. Your book is telling a lie."

The silence in the room was sudden and heavy, broken only by the distant drip of water from the eaves. The other apprentices, scattered around the mill-house, had gone quiet, their hands still resting on their instruments. Joss was leaning against a support beam, his carpenter’s pencil frozen behind his ear, his eyes fixed on Isla’s face with an expression that was part worry and part fascination. Sera Quillon, who had been polishing her silver rule, had stopped moving, the cloth resting on the metal like a small, surrendered flag.

Isla looked at the slate. The numbers were there, black and precise. 4,231. She looked at her field-book. The ink was dry. The figures were clear. 4,321.

"Mags," Isla said, her voice sounding strange to her own ears, as if it belonged to someone else, "are you certain?"

"I am as certain as I can be without a second set of eyes," Mags said. She did not look away, her gaze steady and unblinking. "I think, Isla, that it is yours."
pages.image: In a dim stone mill-house, Mags Okoro, a fifteen-year-old girl with deep-brown skin, short black twists tied with a bright blue scarf, and a teal jacket, stands holding a slate, tapping it with a knuckle while looking at Isla Corrin, who sits at an oak table with a field-book, looking pale.

pages.text:
Isla stared at the page. The ink was hers, the handwriting hers, the steady, meticulous script that Master Vasht had praised so often. But as she looked at the two digits, the three and the two, they seemed to swim, not with motion, but with a terrible, cold stillness. A transposition. A simple, human, fatal slip of the pen. She had written three where two belonged, and two where three had been.

Ninety links. Sixty feet.

The horror did not hit her like a wave. It settled into her bones, cold and heavy, like the stone floor of the Atlas Room at dawn. She thought of the western hillside, the one she had sealed three days ago. The one that had settled with a long, beautiful ripple of light, the land breathing into its new shape. If the traverse was wrong, the hill was wrong. Not just a mark on paper. A physical deformation in the world, a sag in the earth, a river perhaps running uphill, a field tilting into the mud.

Her first instinct was not to speak. It was not even to think. It was a mechanical, animal urge to reach for the eraser, to scrape the ink away, to write the correct number, and to close the book. If she corrected it quietly, no one would know. The traverse would close. The hill would stand. The Guild would see a true sheet. No one would ask how the error had been found, or who had made it. It would be a secret, tucked away in the margin, a flaw smoothed over by the sheer weight of the finished work.

She reached for the eraser. Her hand trembled. She looked at the page, and for a moment, she saw Hester Corrin’s face, not in memory, but in the shadow of her own error. She saw the blank sheet in the Atlas Room, hanging there in the silence, and she understood, with a sharp, clarifying pain, what it meant to hide a mistake. It meant the land remained loose. It meant the people in Ennis Vale remained lost. It meant that the truth was a trap she had built for herself, and she was sitting inside it.

She put the eraser down. Her hand was shaking so badly she could not pick up her pen.
pages.image: Close up on Isla Corrin's light-brown hands, one holding a rubber eraser, the other resting on an open field-book with handwritten numbers, her face above the page showing shock and cold dread, ink stains visible on her fingers.

pages.text:
Isla stood up, the chair legs scraping a harsh, jarring note across the stone floor that seemed to cut the air in two. She did not look at Joss, nor at Sera, nor at the cluster of villagers who had gathered in the mill-yard to listen; her eyes stayed fixed on the table, the slate, and the small, damning error written in her own hand.

"Mags is right," Isla said. Her voice was steady, though it cost her a great deal of effort to keep it that way. "I made a mistake. A transposition. I wrote four thousand three hundred and twenty-one when I meant four thousand two hundred and thirty-one. The difference is ninety links. The western traverse is wrong, and the hill I sealed three days ago is not where it should be."

The silence that followed was absolute, heavy as a held breath. Then a low murmur rippled through the crowd of villagers, a sound like wind moving through dry corn. Perrin Ashdown, tiny and wiry, leaned on his stick, his white whiskers bristling in the dim light. He did not look angry; he looked as though he were waiting for the ink to dry.

Isla took a breath. "I found it because Mags checked the sum. I could have corrected it quietly. I wanted to. But I thought of Hester. I thought of the sheet that was condemned for an error that was not hers. I thought of the Guild, and the benchmarks, and the secrets they keep. And I realized that if I hide this, the land stays loose. If I hide this, I am not a surveyor. I am just a girl who is afraid of being wrong."

Sera Quillon stepped forward. Her plum-purple coat was crisp, her black bob sharp against the shadows, and for the first time her expression was not one of rivalry or judgment, but of genuine astonishment.

"You just told everybody," Sera said, her voice soft.

"Yes," Isla said.

"In front of the people whose land is at stake," Sera continued. "You could have fixed it in the dark. You could have had a private closure. But you are doing this in the light."

"It is not private," Isla said, her gaze steady on the old man. "The work is not private. The land is not private. If I am to fix the error, it must be done where you can see it. Where you can check it. Where you can know that I am not hiding."

Joss stepped out from behind the support beam. He was tall, his sandy hair untidy, his rust-red shirt stained with wood dust. He looked at the slate, then at Isla, and did not say anything; he just nodded, once, a small, firm movement that anchored the moment.

Perrin straightened up, his eyes sharp. He looked at Isla, and then at Mags, and finally at the slate. "Show us the numbers," he said. "All of them. Every leg. Every angle. Do not hide anything."
pages.image: In the dim mill-house, Isla Corrin, in a mustard-yellow coat with two brass pencils in her auburn hair knot, stands addressing a group of villagers, including Old Perrin Ashdown in a patched green coat, while Sera Quillon in a plum-purple velvet coat and Joss Harrowgate in a rust-red work shirt listen with serious, attentive expressions.

pages.text:
The repair was no quick task. It required the sort of patience Isla had learned only through years of holding a line steady while the world tried to pull her off it. She and Mags spent the night re-observing the two stations that bordered the erroneous leg. Rain, fine and cold, had started again. They set up the sightglass on the wet grass, the mud sucking at their boots with a sound like a hungry mouth. Isla held the line, her hand steady despite the chill that seeped through her canvas coat, while Mags read the angles. They worked in silence, the only sounds the soft click of the fine-adjustment screw and the persistent drip of water from the tripod legs.

By dawn, they had the new angles. Isla brought them back to the mill-house, where the villagers were already awake, wrapped in shawls and waiting. The schoolmistress, a woman with sharp eyes and a pencil tucked behind one ear, took the slate and began to check the figures. She did not rush. She checked every addition, every subtraction, and every sine ratio. She verified the declination correction and the baseline projection. Then, with a scrutiny that felt almost surgical, she checked Isla’s work itself.

It took the better part of the day. The villagers brought food, simple things: bread, cheese, and cold porridge that Mags had made the night before. They sat around the table, watching. They did not speak, but they were present, their stillness a steady force in the room. Their presence anchored the heavy barge in a strong current, a good weight that held the room together. Isla felt the trust in the air. It was not blind. It was earned. It was the trust of people who had been lost for forty-four years, and who were watching to see if this girl would make the same mistake again.

Sera helped with the calculations. She used her silver rule to draw the new traverse on a large sheet of paper, spreading the error across the legs in a process she called the honest sharing of a mistake. The numbers balanced out with a precision that felt like a well-tuned instrument. The lines closed. The closure was not perfect, but it was true.

When the schoolmistress finally nodded, the room exhaled. The relief was sharp, mixed with a quiet respect that settled into the air. Isla looked at the sheet, at the new lines, at the corrected traverse. The work was not as clean as she would have liked. It was not as fast. But it was honest. And for the first time in two days, she felt like she could breathe.
pages.image: In the mill-house, the schoolmistress, a woman with sharp eyes and a pencil behind her ear, checks calculations on a slate while Isla Corrin and Mags Okoro watch intently, surrounded by villagers and apprentices, the atmosphere tense but hopeful.

pages.text:
At dawn, the traverse closed.

The total error was four feet over forty-one miles. It was a small number, yet a true one. Isla stood at the table, her hands resting on the edge, and looked at the final figure. A perfect closure was a zero, a myth she had chased through every textbook in the Guild. This was a number she could stand behind.

Master Vasht, who had been brought forward in the wagon, sat in the corner, his ankle propped up on a pillow. He had been watching the work, his grey eyes sharp and focused. He picked up the slate and read the figures. He read them twice. Then he looked up.

"Four feet," he said. "Over forty-one miles. That is a closure of one in fifty thousand."

He looked at Isla, and for a moment, his face was unreadable. Then he smiled, a small, rare smile that reached his eyes. "That is the best closure I have ever seen. In thirty years of practice, I have never seen a traverse close so tightly, with so many variables, under such difficult conditions."

Isla felt a wave of pride, but it was tempered by humility. "It is only so good because it was checked by eleven people," she said. "Mags checked the arithmetic. Sera checked the geometry. The schoolmistress checked the logic. Joss checked the field notes. And I checked my own hand. No one of us was perfect. But together, we were true."

Vasht nodded. He leaned forward, his walking stick resting on his knee. "That is exactly why," he said. "A single surveyor can make a mistake. But a team, a true team, with honest work and shared responsibility, can build a line that holds. That is the secret of the Guild, Isla. Not the ink. Not the instruments. The people. The care. The willingness to be checked."

He looked at the villagers, at the apprentices, at the sheet on the table. "You have fixed the land," he said. "But more importantly, you have fixed the trust. And that is a harder thing to do."

Isla looked at the sheet, at the new lines, at the corrected traverse. It was not just a map. It was a promise. And for the first time, she believed she could keep it.
